To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) symmetry is a fundamental cue in 3-D reconstruction; (2) the homography groups induced by symmetry groups provide a unified theoretical foundation to extract and segment symmetric patterns in images, and to recover the 3-D poses and structures of the symmetric objects; and (3) symmetry cells and complexes are new geometric primitives which can serve as the basic building blocks for 3-D scene reconstruction.

(i) the homography groups induced by the symmetry group of an object are the key to the recovery of 3-D information, (ii) the common spatial relations between symmetric objects provide the key constraints for the extraction of symmetry cells and the matching between cells across different images, and (iii) the symmetry-based segmentation of a single image can be extended to multiple images to achieve 3-D reconstruction.

symmetry is an extremely powerful cue for 3D reconstruction from perspective images, that the 3D geometric information is preserved through perspective imaging, and that a unified theoretical framework can be used to extract and segment multiple symmetric objects present in a single or multiple perspective images.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of 3-D reconstruction of 2-D patterns from perspective images.
developing new algorithms for 3-D scene reconstruction from multiple calibrated images, based on the rich geometric structure information provided by 2-D symmetric objects.
the problem of recovering 3-D geometric and structural information from a set of images.

symmetry is a powerful and effective geometric cue for 2-D segmentation and 3-D structure reconstruction from perspective images.

the framework and algorithms developed in this thesis are a significant step forward toward a unified, systematic, and practical solution to the problem of 3-D reconstruction using symmetry cues from images.

the proposed algorithms and systems provide a new paradigm for the extraction of geometric structures from images, which is more general, accurate, and robust than the conventional point- or line-based methods.
